Hi Lynette,

Part of this answer depends on your research questions. But here are some things that I generally report. 

- In the Method section, I would always reference lavaan and R and any other package that was relevant to your analysis. You can cite lavaan by typing: citation("lavaan") and to cite R type: citation(). You may also want to note the version of the software. I would note the estimation method you used, discuss how you handled missing data, and the number of models/factors you fit.

- In the Results section, it is very common to present global fit indices (e.g., CFI, TLI, and RMSEA), where larger values of CFI and TLI indicate good fit, while lower values of RMSEA do. If you fit different models, you might want a table with these different fit indices to justify your decision to go with one model over another and if your models were nested, i.e. used the same sample covariance-matrix, then you could report chi-square difference tests.

- In the Results section, you could include a table of factor loadings, noting which were significant, or you could create a path diagram. To overcome the issue of constraining the first variable to 1 for identification, you could report the standardized coefficients, std.all, in your table or path diagram. If you have multiple factors, you can report the covariances or correlations between them.

- If you used modification indices, then I would report these paths as well as a justification for why.

Regarding the variance estimates, do you mean the variances of the factors or the indicators? If you report standardized coefficients, then the factor variances are 1 and the variances of the indicators, assuming you have simple structure where each indicator is associated with just a single factor, are just 1 - (std.all coefficients)^2. Similarly, the r-squared for each indicator would just be (std.all coefficent)^2. I don't think you need to report this and probably wouldn't since it can be derived from standardized loadings in the case of simple structure.

Chris
